headline: Great Point's Full of Bait and Boils — Just No Albies Yet
subhead: Terns are working sand eels hard off the Point and stripers are underneath them, but the first false albacore of the year still hasn't turned the corner into the Sound.
body_markdown:
There's a push of sand eels stacked on the rip off Great Point right now thick enough that the terns can't leave it alone, working in tight circles low over the water on the last two hours of the ebb, and under that bait there's bass — good ones, mixed with cocktail blues — punching through the surface in short, violent bursts before going back down. It's the kind of sign that gets your pulse up expecting the first bonito or albie of the season to come ripping through that bait ball. They haven't yet. Not off the Point, not at Sankaty, not out on the Shoals. The water's plenty warm enough — this has been a summer of warm-water signals up and down the coast, with bonito already showing at Block Island and Point Judith and expected to keep pushing this way as September nears — but Nantucket Sound hasn't gotten its invitation yet. Give it another week to ten days before you plan a trip strictly around speedsters.

What you can plan around right now is a solid, honest late-August pattern: stripers in a daytime lull, feeding hard at first light and again after dark, bluefish filling in the gaps everywhere, and fluke that have gone soft and scattered with the warm water pushing them off the open flats and into anything with current and depth. That's the read from the docks in Nantucket and out of Chatham this week, and it lines up with what's happening from the Cape down through the Islands — surface temps are holding high enough that fish are avoiding the sun and doing their business in low light or down in structure.

Great Point is fishing best on the last two hours of the ebb into the start of the flood, with the rip stacking bait against the shoal and stripers holding on the down-current edge in 15 to 25 feet. Sand eel imitations are the call — 3-inch Albie Snax in bone or olive, or a slim epoxy jig worked with a fast, erratic retrieve to match the real thing skittering across the surface. Bluefish are mixed in and will happily eat the same lures, so don't be shocked when something with teeth shortens your leader. A few boats working wire or heavy fluoro up top have done better keeping bass in the mix instead of getting bit off every third cast.

Sankaty's rip has been quieter but more consistent — smaller fish, tighter to the bottom, better on bucktails than surface plugs right now. A half-ounce white bucktail with a chunk of curly-tail trailer, bounced slow along the bottom on the last of the outgoing, has been picking away at schoolie-to-mid-30-inch bass in that stretch. Nothing to write home about, but steady, and steady beats nothing on a week like this.

Monomoy is where the better numbers are coming from. With the wind out of the southwest most of this week, the rips off the south end and around the elbow have been setting up clean — moving water pushing bait against structure, stripers stacked on the seams. Live eels fished after dark on the last two hours of the ebb have been the most reliable producer for the better-class fish, with a few reports of bass pushing past 30 pounds coming off the flats south of the island in the dark hours. During the day, the same water has been giving up bluefish steadily on top-water — a Rebel Jumpin' Minnow or a Hopkins No-Eql worked fast through the current seams will get bit as long as there's bait around, and there has been. Chatham's inlet and the harbor structure have had their share of snapper blues thick in the shallows, a reliable back-bay bite for anyone with kids or a slow afternoon to kill.

Fluke have been the tougher story. With water this warm, the fish have spread out across the flats instead of holding tight, and that's softened catch rates almost everywhere except the deeper edges — the channel drop-offs around Monomoy, the cuts near Nantucket Shoals, and the deeper water off Horseshoe Shoal where a cooler bottom layer still holds. Four-inch white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged slow along bottom on the last of the incoming, have been the most dependable presentation. Don't expect to load the cooler — a few keepers mixed with a lot of shorts has been the honest average this week.

Looking ahead, the moon's building toward full, which should sharpen up the tidal swings and tighten the bite windows at the rips over the next several days — good news for anyone working Great Point or Monomoy on a set tide stage rather than fishing around blind. Southwest wind looks likely to hold into the weekend, which keeps Monomoy's rips in good shape and should keep pushing bait tight against structure there. The bigger question is the exotics. With bonito already stacking up to the west and the warm-water regime showing no signs of breaking yet, the smart bet is that Nantucket Sound gets its first legitimate bonito or albie push sometime in the next one to two weeks, likely showing first out on the Shoals or off Great Point where the bait concentrates hardest. Keep a light spinning rod rigged with small metal in the rocket launcher just in case — when they show, they don't give much notice.
